drills.title: vs Maremgot (746) — Scotch Game
drills.coachNote: White's plan is f3-f4, simplifying the pawns so his king gets time to scramble instead of getting shut out. Your d5 doesn't stop that at all — White gets in f4, you're forced to recapture gxf4, and his king slips to a2 while your bishop has to babysit e7, giving back a slice of a completely won position. Ke3 keeps the king marching straight at the target instead: Ke3, Kc2, a5, Kb1 and your king simply strolls in and grabs the f3 pawn with Kxf3. When you're this far up, walk the king toward the weakness first — pawn pushes can wait.
drills.threat: White's f3-pawn wants to push to f4, trading off your kingside pawns before your king can march over and trap his.

drills.coachNote: Same idea one move earlier: White wants f3-f4 to simplify before you can cut his king off, and every move you spend elsewhere is a move he gets to make it happen. Kd4 heads toward the queenside instead, so White gets f4 in for free — gxf4, Kc2, f3, and his king escapes to consolidate while your kingside majority stops meaning much. Ke5 heads the right direction: Ke5, Kc2, Kf4 puts your king right next to White's pawns, and by Kd3-Ke2 you're deep in his position with the pawns falling. The lesson is the same — race your king to the weak pawns before your opponent gets to trade them away.
drills.threat: White is one tempo from f3-f4, and once those pawns trade off his king gets time to run and dig in.

drills.coachNote: Black's whole idea is simple: Bxg4 just wins your queen for a bishop, since nothing covers that diagonal from c8. Rad1 is a quiet centralizing move that ignores the emergency — Black plays Bxg4, hxg4, Re8 and you're down a queen for a bishop in a position that was roughly balanced. Ne7+ solves the problem with tempo instead: the check forks Kg8 and Qf8, so after Kg7 you get to swing the queen to e4, off the hanging square and centralized, and you're already picking up material — Bxb2 Qxa8 nets you a whole rook. Before any quiet developing move, always ask whether your most valuable piece is actually defended.
drills.threat: Your queen on g4 sits on the same diagonal as Black's bishop on c8, completely undefended.

drills.coachNote: You're already down a rook in this ending, and Black's real plan is Re2+ followed by doubling on the second rank to run your king out of squares. Pushing c4 ignores that completely — Re2+ forces Ka3, then Rgg2 doubles the rooks right where you needed to defend, and the position collapses further from merely lost to hopeless. Rf2 covers that key second-rank square first: after Rf2 Re1, Ka3 Ke6, you're still worse but the rooks can't just walk in for free, and you keep some practical fighting chances. When you're down material, plugging the entry square comes before pushing pawns.

Rf4+! is the move that changes the story — check first. After Ke3 Rf1 you're already crashing into the back rank, and Rxe2 Re8+ Kd4 keeps White's king running. You grabbed the loose knight with Rxf4, pulling your other rook off f8 — the very piece guarding e8 — and White answered Qxe8+, winning the exchange with check; after Kh7 Qe6 he was mopping up, a six-pawn swing from equal to lost. Qxf4 wins the same free knight but leaves your rook on f8 exactly where it needs to be, so after Qe2 Rf5 Rad1 Qg5 Rfe1 the game stays balanced instead of collapsing. Before grabbing a hanging piece, always check what the capturing piece was defending.
